arXiv:2607.10102v2 [math.PR] 21 Sep 2026

Dynamical mean-field limit and replica-symmetric free energy for the orthogonally-invariant SK model

Zhou Fan , Theodor Misiakiewicz , Leda Wang and Garrett G. Wen Address: Yale University, Department of Statistics and Data Science Email address: zhou.fan@yale.edu Email address: theodor.misiakiewicz@yale.edu Email address: leda.wang@yale.edu Email address: gang.wen@yale.edu
Abstract.

We study a class of diffusion processes on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} interacting through a symmetric matrix 𝐗∈ℝn×n\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}. When eigenvectors of 𝐗\mathbf{X} are random and uniformly distributed on the orthogonal group, we derive a dynamical mean-field limit for the empirical law of sample paths, extending a classical characterization due to Sompolinsky and Zippelius for 𝐗∼GOE\mathbf{X}\sim\operatorname{GOE}. This limit takes the form of a generalized Langevin equation with correlated Gaussian noise and memory, whose correlation and response kernels relate to those of the original diffusion process through a system of convolution equations depending on 𝐗\mathbf{X} via the free cumulants of its eigenvalue distribution.

Specializing to the overdamped Langevin diffusion {𝜽t}t≥0\{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} for a Gibbs measure

μ⁡(𝜽)∝exp⁡(12​𝜽⊤​𝐗​𝜽)​∏i=1nν⁡(d​θi),\mu(\boldsymbol{\theta})\propto\exp\Big(\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}\Big)\prod_{i=1}^{n}\nu(\mathrm{d}\theta_{i}),

we analyze this mean-field limit under an assumption that the dynamics are rapidly mixing. In this regime, the correlation/response kernels admit time-translation-invariant approximants which satisfy a fluctuation-dissipation relation. The generalized Langevin equation admits a Markovian approximation with coupling to an auxiliary multivariate OU-process, and converges in time to a replica-symmetric prediction for the empirical law of coordinates under μ\mu. The correlation structure of the auxiliary process may be understood through the infinitesimal generator of a Markov semigroup for the lifted process of path histories 𝝃t={𝜽s}s:s≤t\boldsymbol{\xi}^{t}=\{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}\}_{s:s\leq t}.

Consequently, we show that the free energy of the Gibbs measure converges to a replica-symmetric limit under an explicit high-temperature condition, which for an Ising model is

‖𝐗‖op<1/2.\|\mathbf{X}\|_{\mathrm{op}}<1/2.

By recent dynamical universality results, this implies that the same characterization of the free energy holds in fully deterministic models without random disorder, as long as 𝐗\mathbf{X} satisfies a set of deterministic delocalization conditions.

1. Introduction

Let 𝐗∈ℝn×n\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} be a (deterministic or random) symmetric matrix. Consider a diffusion process or gradient flow in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} interacting through 𝐗\mathbf{X},

(1.1) d​𝜽t=[f⁡(𝜽t)+𝐗​𝜽t]​d​t+2​γ​d​𝐛t\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}=[f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t})+\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}]\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{b}^{t}

where ff is a scalar function applied coordinate-wise. Under suitable mean-field assumptions for 𝐗\mathbf{X} to be specified, the first goal of our work is to obtain an asymptotic characterization of the empirical distribution of coordinates of (1.1) in the limit n→∞n\to\infty. Applying this characterization to study Langevin dynamics for the Gibbs measure

(1.2) μ⁡(d​𝜽)=1𝒵​exp⁡(12​𝜽⊤​𝐗​𝜽)​∏i=1nν⁡(d​θi),\mu(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta})=\frac{1}{\mathcal{Z}}\exp\Big(\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}\Big)\prod_{i=1}^{n}\nu(\mathrm{d}\theta_{i}),

the second goal of our work is to obtain an asymptotic characterization of the free energy and replica overlaps of (1.2) in a regime where these dynamics are rapidly mixing.

For models where 𝐗\mathbf{X} has independent Gaussian entries up to transposition symmetry, such questions are richly studied in the physics and mathematics literatures on spin glasses and disordered systems. A dynamical mean-field limit for a prototypical example of (1.1) was first derived by Sompolinsky and Zippelius in [64], and is given by the law of a scalar generalized Langevin equation

(1.3) d​θt=[f⁡(θt)+∫0tRθ​(t,s)​θs​𝑑s+gt]​𝑑t+2​γ​d​bt,{gt}∼GP⁡(0,Cθ),\mathrm{d}\theta^{t}=\left[f(\theta^{t})+\int_{0}^{t}R_{\theta}(t,s)\theta^{s}\mathrm{d}s+g^{t}\right]\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\mathrm{d}b^{t},\qquad\{g^{t}\}\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,C_{\theta}),

with correlated Gaussian noise {gt}\{g^{t}\} and self-consistently defined correlation and response kernels (Cθ,Rθ)(C_{\theta},R_{\theta}). Convergence in empirical law of the sample paths of (1.1) to (1.3), and an associated annealed large deviations principle, was first proved mathematically by Ben Arous and Guionnet in [3, 40]. The Ising case of the Gibbs measure (1.2) with ν⁡(d​θ)\nu(\mathrm{d}\theta) supported on {±1}\{\pm 1\} corresponds to the classical Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (S-K) model [63], for which the form of the asymptotic free energy was famously conjectured by Parisi in [60] and proved by Guerra and Talagrand [39, 67]; we refer to [68, 69, 58] for textbook treatments of this model and its rich history. Universality over classes of random matrices 𝐗\mathbf{X} having independent non-Gaussian entries (up to symmetry) has been shown for the free energy of the S-K model in [12] and for dynamics similar to (1.1) in [18, 20].

Arguably, this universality class of disorder matrices with independent entries remains quite limited, raising a question of whether analogous results hold under more general mean-field structure. In this work, we aim to extend some of these developments to a class of disorder matrices 𝐗∈ℝn×n\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} that are orthogonally-invariant in law — i.e. whose matrix of eigenvectors is uniformly distributed on the orthogonal group — and to an associated universality class that encompasses examples of deterministic matrices 𝐗\mathbf{X}. Our contributions are threefold:

  1. 1.

    For the dynamics (1.1) with orthogonally-invariant 𝐗∈ℝn×n\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} having a compactly supported asymptotic spectral law Λ\Lambda, we develop an extension of the mean-field limit (1.3).

    This extension has the same structural form as (1.3),

    (1.4) d​θt=[f⁡(θt)+∫0tRg​(t,s)​θs​𝑑s+gt]​𝑑t+2​γ​d​bt,{gt}∼GP⁡(0,Cg),\mathrm{d}\theta^{t}=\left[f(\theta^{t})+\int_{0}^{t}R_{g}(t,s)\theta^{s}\mathrm{d}s+g^{t}\right]\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\mathrm{d}b^{t},\qquad\{g^{t}\}\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,C_{g}),

    with correlation and response kernels (Cg,Rg)(C_{g},R_{g}) now defined from the kernels (Cθ,Rθ)(C_{\theta},R_{\theta}) which characterize the correlation and response of {𝜽t}t≥0\{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} via convolution equations and the free cumulants of Λ\Lambda (cf. Definition 2.3). We establish almost-sure convergence of the empirical law of sample paths of (1.1) to this limit, when ff has bounded derivatives up to 3rd3^{\text{rd}} order.

  2. 2.

    We carry out an analysis of this mean-field limit (1.4) for the overdamped Langevin dynamics of the Gibbs measure (1.2) when ν⁡(d​θ)=e−U⁡(θ)​d​θ\nu(\mathrm{d}\theta)=e^{-U(\theta)}\mathrm{d}\theta has a smooth potential, under an assumption that these dynamics converge at an exponential dimension-free rate from both an equilibrium and an independent random initialization (cf. Assumption 2.5).

    In this dynamical regime, we prove that the preceding kernels (Cg,Rg)(C_{g},R_{g}) have time-translation-invariant limits (cg,rg)(c_{g},r_{g}) as t→∞t\to\infty, which satisfy a fluctuation-dissipation relation

    (1.5) rg​(t)=−cg′​(t).r_{g}(t)={-}c_{g}^{\prime}(t).

    In contrast to the mean-field limit of Sompolinsky-Zippelius in (1.3), the correlation kernel cg​(⋅)c_{g}(\cdot) may not have a mixture-of-exponentials form. We instead establish a sequence of approximations cg​(t)≈um⊤​e−t​Am​umc_{g}(t)\approx u_{m}^{\top}e^{-tA_{m}}u_{m} with non-diagonal, asymmetric matrices Am∈ℝm×mA_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}, leading to a sequence of Markovian approximations of (1.4),

    (1.6) d​θt\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\theta^{t} =[f⁡(θt)+um⊤​xt+z]​d​t+2​d​bt\displaystyle=[f(\theta^{t})+u_{m}^{\top}x^{t}+z]\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}b^{t}
    d​xt\displaystyle\mathrm{d}x^{t} =−Am​[xt−um​θt]​d​t+Σm​d​bxt.\displaystyle={-}A_{m}[x^{t}-u_{m}\theta^{t}]\mathrm{d}t+\Sigma_{m}\,\mathrm{d}b_{x}^{t}.

    Via these approximations, we show that {θt}t≥0\{\theta^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} in (1.4) converges to an equilibrium law that coincides with a replica-symmetric prediction for the empirical distribution of coordinates under the Gibbs measure (1.2).

  3. 3.

    A sufficient condition ensuring Assumption 2.5 is a log-Sobolev inequality for the Gibbs measure, which may be verified under an explicit high-temperature condition [6]. From this, we prove replica-symmetric limits for the overlaps and free energy of (1.2).

    Concretely, for the Ising model with ν⁡(d​θ)∝eh​δθ=1+e−h​δθ=−1\nu(\mathrm{d}\theta)\propto e^{h}\delta_{\theta=1}+e^{-h}\delta_{\theta=-1} where h∈ℝh\in\mathbb{R} is an external field, we establish this result under the high-temperature assumption

    (1.7) ‖𝐗‖op<1/2.\|\mathbf{X}\|_{\mathrm{op}}<1/2.

    (In the setting of the classical S-K model where 𝐗=β​𝐉\mathbf{X}=\beta\mathbf{J} and 𝐉∼GOE⁡(n)\mathbf{J}\sim\operatorname{GOE}(n), this corresponds to the assumption β<1/4\beta<1/4, which is a subset of the full replica-symmetric regime [49].) Leveraging the dynamical universality results of [26, 71], we deduce that the same conclusion holds when h=0h=0 for a general class of purely deterministic matrices 𝐗∈ℝn×n\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} satisfying delocalization conditions (cf. Assumption 2.9), and for arbitrary h∈ℝh\in\mathbb{R} when 𝐗\mathbf{X} is a “semi-random” matrix conjugated by a diagonal matrix of random {±1}\{\pm 1\} signs.

These results are presented in Section 2.

1.1. Existing literature

Dynamics. The form of the mean-field limit (1.4) for the diffusion equation (1.1) with orthogonally-invariant 𝐗\mathbf{X} may be anticipated from the analysis of Opper, Çakmak, and Winther [55], who computed the dynamical mean-field equations for an analogous class of discrete-time dynamics. The mean-field limit (1.4) and convolutional structure of its correlation and response kernels may be understood as a passage of this result to continuous time.

A particular class of discrete-time dynamics — analogous to Approximate Message Passing (AMP) algorithms [43, 24] and TAP iterations [9] in models with Gaussian disorder 𝐗\mathbf{X} — was highlighted in [55] as having purely Gaussian limiting dynamics. For this AMP class, convergence to the mean-field limit was proved mathematically in [35], extending an approach of iterative conditioning of Haar-orthogonal matrices previously developed in [50, 66, 61] to analyze a simpler family of divergence-free “vector-AMP” algorithms. Alternative proofs and extensions of the result of [35] have since been obtained in [48, 38], and universality over semi-random and deterministic disorder matrices 𝐗\mathbf{X} has been shown in increasingly general contexts in [26, 71, 38].

It was shown by Celentano, Cheng, and Montanari [13], in an analogous statistical model with i.i.d. Gaussian disorder, that the mean-field limit of general discrete-time iterative algorithms may be deduced from that of AMP, and also that the mean-field limit of continuous-time gradient flow dynamics may be proved using an approach different from [3, 40]. This approach relies on a reduction to AMP dynamics via time-discretization, and a passage to the continuous-time limit through verifying contractivity of the dynamical fixed-point equations in a suitably defined Banach metric. The approach has been extended to derive mean-field limits for broad families of discrete-time iterative algorithms in [37, 41, 14, 16] and for continuous-time Langevin diffusions and stochastic gradient dynamics in [30, 33, 54]. We apply a similar proof strategy in our work, to pass the characterization of AMP in [35] to continuous time.

Mathematical analysis of aging in the dynamical mean-field limit of a spherical 2-spin model was carried out in [2], of convergence in time of the Cugliandolo-Kurchan/Crisanti-Horner-Sommers equations of the spherical p-spin model to an FDT equilibrium in [19], and of convergence in time of these equations under disorder-dependent initial conditions in [21, 22]. For non-spherical models, aging dynamics and their connection to the static replica-symmetry-breaking structure of the Gibbs mesaures was analyzed using (non-rigorous) statistical physics techniques in [1]. A mathematical analysis for a non-spherical model with Gaussian disorder was carried out in [31] in a dynamical rapid-mixing regime similar to our work; we build upon several ideas of [31], discussed in Section 1.2.

Free energy. The Ising case of the model (1.2) was introduced by Marinari, Parisi, and Ritort [52] as a model which may exhibit similar mean-field phenomena as models with deterministic disorder. Replica-symmetric and 1-RSB predictions for the asymptotic free energy of this model were computed in [52, 15]. TAP equations for the magnetization were derived in [59] using a high-temperature expansion and in [56] using an alternative cavity method. [51] extended the former analysis to a broad class of statistical models with orthogonally-invariant random disorder, and discussed its connection to dynamical algorithms.

Mathematical proofs of such predictions remain scarce in the literature, even in high temperature. For a high-temperature regime of the Ising model without external field, where quenched and annealed free energies coincide, a replica-symmetric limit for the free energy was proved in [8] using the second-moment method. This was extended to an Ising model with external field h∈ℝh\in\mathbb{R} in [34] via a conditional second-moment method analogous to that of [10] for the S-K model and [23] for the Ising perceptron, conditioning on the filtration of a TAP iteration for computing the magnetization. This result of [34] showed, for 𝐗=β​𝐉\mathbf{X}=\beta\mathbf{J} where the asymptotic spectral law of 𝐉\mathbf{J} converges to Λ¯\bar{\Lambda}, that the free energy converges to its replica-symmetric prediction under a high-temperature condition of the form β∈(0,β0)\beta\in(0,\beta_{0}) for some

β0≡β0​(Law⁡(Λ¯)).\beta_{0}\equiv\beta_{0}(\operatorname{Law}(\bar{\Lambda})).

As the analysis of the second-moment variational problem in [34] was perturbative around β=0\beta=0, it is difficult to glean a more explicit bound for β0\beta_{0}, and we believe that this bound would be substantially smaller than our explicit guarantee in (1.7). In a related statistical generalized linear model with orthogonally-invariant design, replica-symmetric predictions for the free energy were derived in [44, 65]. This was proved mathematically for a linear model with design factorizable through Gaussian randomness in [5], via a Gaussian interpolation approach. The replica-symmetric ground state energy for convex potentials was also proved in [36] via analysis of a vector AMP algorithm for convex optimization.

One perspective on the challenge of using a dynamical approach to prove properties of the Gibbs measure is in certifying the optimality of the dynamics. For example, in the context of (1.2) and related statistical models, AMP algorithms/TAP iterations that conjecturally converge to the magnetization are known [55, 61, 11], but this convergence has thus far only been certified in high-temperature regimes analogous to that of [34], relying on a-priori understanding of the asymptotic free energy and structure of the Gibbs measure [32, 47]. Likewise, while mean-field characterizations of the ground state energy in convex landscapes may be established by certifying optimality of optimization algorithms through a first-order condition [7, 25, 36], certifying global optimality of such algorithms in non-convex landscapes remains challenging. In this work, we take an approach of analyzing the standard overdamped Langevin dynamics, which has a more complex dynamical mean-field limit than AMP-type algorithms, but whose convergence to the Gibbs measure may be certified through entropy-decay arguments external to the mean-field theory.

As a benefit of our dynamical approach to analyzing the free energy, our results inherit the aforementioned universality over semi-random and deterministic matrices 𝐗\mathbf{X} [26, 71, 38], which has been shown for algorithm dynamics but not yet for static properties of the Gibbs measure. Our results confirm that disordered-systems characterizations of the Gibbs measure can hold for systems without random disorder, as originally anticipated by [52].

1.2. Proof ideas

We describe briefly the main ideas of our analyses.

As discussed in the preceding section, (1.4) is obtained by passing a characterization of a discrete-time AMP algorithm in [55, 35] to continuous time. An important distinction between these discrete-time and continuous-time characterizations is that the correlation/response kernels of the former are defined iteratively/inductively over time. The first contribution of our work is to formalize a sense in which the continuous-time kernels Cθ,Rθ,Cg,RgC_{\theta},R_{\theta},C_{g},R_{g} may instead be understood as the fixed points of a contractive map.

An obstacle to this formalization is that the convolutional equations mapping

(1.8) (Cθ,Rθ)↦(Cg,Rg)(C_{\theta},R_{\theta})\mapsto(C_{g},R_{g})

do not, in general, ensure that CgC_{g} remains a positive-semidefinite (p.s.d.) kernel, which is needed to define the process (1.4); thus, it is a bit unclear on what domain such a contractive map should be defined. A related issue is that even when CgC_{g} is p.s.d., it seems challenging to analyze contractivity of (1.8) under a Wasserstein-coupling metric for Cθ,CgC_{\theta},C_{g} as used in the arguments of [13, 30, 33]. We resolve these issues by formalizing the fixed-point interpretation of the dynamical mean-field limit via a sequence of mappings

(Cθ,Rθ)↦(Cg,Rg)↦𝒫⁡(Cg,Rg)↦(Cθ,Rθ),(C_{\theta},R_{\theta})\mapsto(C_{g},R_{g})\mapsto\mathcal{P}(C_{g},R_{g})\mapsto(C_{\theta},R_{\theta}),

where 𝒫\mathcal{P} projects CgC_{g} under an alternative weighted L2L^{2} metric onto a subset of the p.s.d. cone. We then develop different arguments to establish contractivity in this metric, and leverage results of [35] to show that at the fixed point of these mappings, CgC_{g} is in fact p.s.d., and thus is also a fixed point without projection by 𝒫\mathcal{P}.

Turning to the analysis of the overdamped Langevin equation, from the assumed convergence condition in Assumption 2.5 and an identification of (Cθ,Rθ)(C_{\theta},R_{\theta}) as the limits of coordinate-wise correlation and response functions of {𝜽t}t≥0\{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0}, one may deduce the existence of time-translation-invariant limits cθ,rθc_{\theta},r_{\theta} for these kernels at large times, together with their fluctuation-dissipation relation

(1.9) rθ​(t)=−cθ′​(t)r_{\theta}(t)={-}c_{\theta}^{\prime}(t)

(Lemma 4.1). These arguments are similar to [31] which analyzed a statistical model with Gaussian disorder. Interestingly, we are able to verify that (1.9) implies also the fluctuation-dissipation relation rg​(t)=−cg′​(t)r_{g}(t)={-}c_{g}^{\prime}(t) corresponding to the kernels Cg,RgC_{g},R_{g} appearing in the generalized Langevin equation (1.4). This verification is a short calculation in the Fourier domain (Lemma 4.2).

We show that cg​(⋅)c_{g}(\cdot) may be interpreted as the large-nn limit of the correlation function of coordinates of

𝐠t=𝐗​𝜽t−∫−∞trg​(t−s)​𝜽s​𝑑s\mathbf{g}^{t}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}-\int_{-\infty}^{t}r_{g}(t-s)\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}\mathrm{d}s

at equilibrium, which are observables of the full path history 𝝃t:={𝜽s}s:s≤t\boldsymbol{\xi}^{t}:=\{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}\}_{s:s\leq t}. As this “lifted” process {𝝃t}t∈ℝ\{\boldsymbol{\xi}^{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{R}} remains Markovian over this space of path histories, writing ν\nu for its stationary measure and {Pt}t≥0\{P_{t}\}_{t\geq 0} for its L2​(ν)L^{2}(\nu)-semigroup, this implies a representation

cg​(t)=limn→∞1n​𝔼ν​[f⊤​Pt​f]c_{g}(t)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\,\mathbb{E}_{\nu}[f^{\top}P_{t}f]

where ff is the function for which 𝐠t=f⁡(𝝃t)\mathbf{g}^{t}=f(\boldsymbol{\xi}^{t}). An important distinction with the setting of Gaussian disorder is that here {Pt}t≥0\{P_{t}\}_{t\geq 0} is irreversible, and its infinitesimal generator is not self-adjoint on L2​(ν)L^{2}(\nu). Thus, we do not obtain from this representation a mixture-of-exponentials form for cg​(⋅)c_{g}(\cdot), and in general, we do not expect such a form to hold true. Instead, we establish an approximation

cg​(t)≈um⊤​e−t​Am​umc_{g}(t)\approx u_{m}^{\top}e^{-tA_{m}}u_{m}

where −Am∈ℝm×m{-}A_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} is a (non-diagonal, asymmetric) matrix that constitutes a finite-dimensional approximation for the generator of {Pt}t≥0\{P_{t}\}_{t\geq 0}. Together with the fluctuation-dissipation relation (1.5), this leads to the previously stated Markov approximation (1.6) for (1.4).

Finally, we show convergence of (1.4) to an equilibrium law characterized by replica-symmetric fixed point equations, by analyzing convergence of the Markovian system (1.6) together with its approximation error for (1.4). The primary technical challenge is that the generator −A{-}A for the above semigroup {Pt}t≥0\{P_{t}\}_{t\geq 0} has non-trivial (in fact, dense) null space in L2​(ν)L^{2}(\nu), and thus the spectral gap of its approximant −Am{-}A_{m} must vanish with the approximation error. Thus, it seems challenging to prove convergence to equilibrium of the Markovian system (1.6) over a fixed time horizon that is independent of this error and the dimension mm; on the other hand, the accumulated approximation error over a mm-dependent time horizon may not be small under a naive coupling and Grönwall argument. We circumvent this issue by using a careful construction of −Am{-}A_{m} that instead approximates a slightly damped version of −A{-}A, and that allows for a stable coupling of (1.4) and (1.6) over an arbitrarily long time horizon on which (1.6) is guaranteed to converge (Corollary 5.2, Lemma 5.3). This implies the replica-symmetric characterization of the Gibbs measure (1.2) under Assumption 2.5, for laws ν\nu having a smooth potential. The concrete implication for the Ising model is then deduced by verifying Assumption 2.5 using the log-Sobolev inequality of [6] for a sequence of double-well potentials that converge to the Ising law.

2. Main results

2.1. Dynamical mean-field limit

Let {𝜽t}t≥0\{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} be a diffusion process on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} taking the form

(2.1) d​𝜽t=[f⁡(𝜽t)+𝐗​𝜽t]​d​t+2​γ​d​𝐛t\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}=[f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t})+\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}]\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{b}^{t}

where 𝐗∈ℝn×n\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is a symmetric matrix, f:ℝ→ℝf:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is a Lipschitz-continuous function applied coordinate-wise, and {𝐛t}t≥0\{\mathbf{b}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} is a standard Brownian motion on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. The case γ=0\gamma=0 corresponds to gradient flow.

Our first main result establishes a deterministic limit, as n→∞n\to\infty, of the empirical distribution of coordinate sample paths

{(θit)t∈[0,T]}i=1n\{(\theta_{i}^{t})_{t\in[0,T]}\}_{i=1}^{n}

for any fixed time horizon T>0T>0 independent of nn. For expositional clarity, let us first state this result for the following class of random disorder matrices 𝐗\mathbf{X} that are orthogonally invariant in law; we discuss universality over the disorder in Section 2.3.

Assumption 2.1.

𝐗=𝐎​𝚲​𝐎⊤\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{O}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{O}^{\top}, where 𝐎∼Haar⁡(𝕆⁡(n))\mathbf{O}\sim\operatorname{Haar}(\mathbb{O}(n)) is a Haar-uniform random matrix on the orthogonal group, and 𝚲=diag⁡(λ1,…,λn)\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n}) is a (deterministic or random) diagonal matrix independent of 𝐎\mathbf{O}. There exists a constant Λmax>0\Lambda_{\max}>0 such that almost surely for all large nn,

‖𝐗‖op≤Λmax.\|\mathbf{X}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\Lambda_{\max}.

Furthermore, there exists a random variable Λ\Lambda (supported on [−Λmax,Λmax][-\Lambda_{\max},\Lambda_{\max}]) with 𝔼⁡[Λ]=0\mathbb{E}[\Lambda]=0 and Var⁡[Λ]>0\operatorname{Var}[\Lambda]>0 such that almost surely as n→∞n\to\infty,

1n​∑i=1nδλi→Law⁡(Λ)​ weakly.\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\delta_{\lambda_{i}}\to\operatorname{Law}(\Lambda)\text{ weakly.}

Throughout, we denote by {κp}p≥2\{\kappa_{p}\}_{p\geq 2} the free cumulants of this random variable Λ\Lambda.

We impose, in addition, the following assumptions on the dynamics (2.1).

Assumption 2.2.
  1. (a)

    f:ℝ→ℝf:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is fixed for all nn, and three-times continuously-differentiable with uniformly bounded first, second, and third derivatives.

  2. (b)

    γ≥0\gamma\geq 0 is a fixed scalar parameter, and the Brownian motion {𝐛t}t≥0\{\mathbf{b}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} is independent of 𝐗\mathbf{X}.

  3. (c)

2.3. Universality over the disorder

Orthogonal invariance of the disorder matrix 𝐗\mathbf{X} in Assumption 2.1 underlies a mean-field characterization of a discrete-time AMP algorithm in [35], from which the dynamical mean-field limit in Theorem 2.4 and results for the Gibbs measure in Theorem 2.6 and Corollaries 2.7 and 2.8 are derived.

It has been shown, in increasing generality in [26, 71, 38], that this characterization holds more broadly over universality classes of (possibly deterministic) matrices 𝐗∈ℝn×n\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}. This implies, as a consequence, that our preceding results carry over to such universality classes.

We provide here a concrete statement of universality for one such class of deterministic disorder matrices 𝐗\mathbf{X} studied in [26, 71].

Assumption 2.9.

Let 𝐗∈ℝn×n\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} be a deterministic symmetric matrix such that ‖𝐗‖op≤Λmax\|\mathbf{X}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\Lambda_{\max} for a constant Λmax>0\Lambda_{\max}>0, and there exists a random variable Λ\Lambda with 𝔼⁡[Λ]=0\mathbb{E}[\Lambda]=0 and Var⁡[Λ]>0\operatorname{Var}[\Lambda]>0 such that as n→∞n\to\infty, the empirical eigenvalue distribution of 𝐗\mathbf{X} satisfies

1n​∑i=1nδλi​(𝐗)→Law⁡(Λ)​ weakly.\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\delta_{\lambda_{i}(\mathbf{X})}\to\operatorname{Law}(\Lambda)\text{ weakly}.

Furthermore, for each fixed integer k≥1k\geq 1, any constant ε>0\varepsilon>0, and all large n≥n0​(ε,k)n\geq n_{0}(\varepsilon,k),

maxi=1n|(𝐗k)i​i−1nTr𝐗k|<n−1/2+ε,maxi≠j|(𝐗k)i​j|<n−1/2+ε.\max_{i=1}^{n}\left|(\mathbf{X}^{k})_{ii}-\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{Tr}\mathbf{X}^{k}\right|<n^{-1/2+\varepsilon},\qquad\max_{i\neq j}\left|(\mathbf{X}^{k})_{ij}\right|<n^{-1/2+\varepsilon}.

For example, one may take 𝐗=β​𝐌\mathbf{X}=\beta\mathbf{M} where β∈ℝ\beta\in\mathbb{R} and 𝐌\mathbf{M} is a Hadamard matrix (with nn a power of 2) or the sine transform

𝐌=(2n+1​sin⁡π​i​jn+1)i,j=1n.\mathbf{M}=\left(\sqrt{\frac{2}{n+1}}\sin\frac{\pi ij}{n+1}\right)_{i,j=1}^{n}.

In either case, 𝐌\mathbf{M} is orthogonal, and Assumption 2.9 holds with Λmax=|β|\Lambda_{\max}=|\beta| and Λ=12​δβ+12​δ−β\Lambda=\frac{1}{2}\delta_{\beta}+\frac{1}{2}\delta_{-\beta}.

Corollary 2.10.

Suppose 𝐗\mathbf{X} satisfies Assumption 2.9.

  1. (a)

    If Assumption 2.2 holds, f:ℝ→ℝf:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is odd, and θ0\theta^{0} is sign invariant in law (i.e. f⁡(x)=−f⁡(−x)f(x)={-}f(-x) for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, and Law⁡(θ0)=Law⁡(−θ0)\operatorname{Law}(\theta^{0})=\operatorname{Law}({-}\theta^{0})), then Theorem 2.4 holds for the dynamics {𝜽t}t≥0\{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0}.

  2. (b)

    If U⁡(⋅)U(\cdot) and Λ\Lambda satisfy all conditions of Corollary 2.7, and U:ℝ→ℝU:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is even (i.e. U⁡(x)=U⁡(−x)U(x)=U(-x) for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}), then all statements of Theorem 2.6 hold for μGibbs\mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}}.

  3. (c)

    If h=0h=0 in the Ising model (2.21) and Λmax<1/2\Lambda_{\max}<1/2, then all statements of Corollary 2.8 hold.

  4. (d)

    If f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot) is not odd, θ0\theta^{0} is not sign-invariant in law, U⁡(⋅)U(\cdot) is not even, or h≠0h\neq 0, then the same conclusions hold for the dynamics and Gibbs measures defined with 𝐒𝐗𝐒\mathbf{S}\mathbf{X}\mathbf{S} in place of 𝐗\mathbf{X}, where 𝐒\mathbf{S} is a diagonal matrix of i.i.d. Rademacher ±1\pm 1 signs independent of 𝜽0\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0} and {𝐛t}t≥0\{\mathbf{b}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0}.

Remark 2.11.

Let 𝐗=(Id−1n​𝟏𝟏⊤)​𝐇​(Id−1n​𝟏𝟏⊤)\mathbf{X}=(\mathrm{Id}-\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top})\mathbf{H}(\mathrm{Id}-\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}) be a “puncturing” of a deterministic matrix 𝐇\mathbf{H} satisfying the conditions of Assumption 2.9, and let 𝐗~=(Id−1n​𝟏𝟏⊤)​𝐇~​(Id−1n​𝟏𝟏⊤)\tilde{\mathbf{X}}=(\mathrm{Id}-\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top})\tilde{\mathbf{H}}(\mathrm{Id}-\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}) be a similar puncturing of an orthogonally-invariant random matrix 𝐇~\tilde{\mathbf{H}} satisfying Assumption 2.1 with the same spectral limit Law⁡(Λ)\operatorname{Law}(\Lambda). One may also verify using [71, Proposition 2.7, Lemma B.1] and the recent result of [38, Theorem 5.3] that, even if f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot) is not odd / U⁡(⋅)U(\cdot) is not even, the mean-field limits for the dynamics {𝜽t}t≥0\{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} and Gibbs measure μGibbs\mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}} coincide for 𝐗\mathbf{X} and 𝐗~\tilde{\mathbf{X}}.

However, without further assumptions for f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot) / U⁡(⋅)U(\cdot) such as the sign symmetry conditions in Corollary 2.10 above, these limits would, in general, be different from those stated in Theorems 2.4 and 2.6 for the unpunctured orthogonally-invariant matrix 𝐇~\tilde{\mathbf{H}}. It is possible to derive analogues of our results for this puncturing of 𝐇~\tilde{\mathbf{H}}, but for brevity we will not do so in the current work.

The remainder of this paper proves the preceding results. Section 3 proves Theorem 2.4 on the dynamical mean-field limit, Section 4 analyzes the kernels Cθ,Rθ,Cg,RgC_{\theta},R_{\theta},C_{g},R_{g} for the overdamped Langevin diffusion at equilibrium, Section 5 proves Theorem 2.6 and Corollaries 2.7 and 2.8 on the Gibbs measure, and Section 6 proves Corollary 2.10 on universality over the disorder.

3. Dynamical mean-field limit

In this section, we prove Theorem 2.4. We will omit arguments that are similar to ones in [30] for brevity, and focus on the differences in our setting of a non-Gaussian disorder matrix 𝐗\mathbf{X}.

Then Theorem 2.4(a) holds upon setting 𝒮θ+\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{+} as the space of kernels (Cθ,Rθ)(C_{\theta},R_{\theta}) on [0,∞)×[0,∞)[0,\infty)\times[0,\infty) whose restrictions to [0,T]×[0,T][0,T]\times[0,T] belong to 𝒮θ+​(T,∅)\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{+}(T,\emptyset) for each T>0T>0, and similarly for 𝒮g+\mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}. ∎

4. Analyses of correlation and response

In this section, we specialize the dynamical mean-field limit of Theorem 2.4 to the overdamped Langevin equation (2.11). Our analysis relies on several important structural properties of the kernels Cθ,Rθ,Cg,RgC_{\theta},R_{\theta},C_{g},R_{g} at large times. We collect these properties in the following two lemmas.

First, under Assumption 2.5, we have the following properties for Cθ,RθC_{\theta},R_{\theta}, including the existence of time-translation-invariant limits cθ,rθ:ℝ→ℝc_{\theta},r_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} for these kernels as t→∞t\to\infty, and a fluctuation-dissipation relation between these limits.

    The Gibbs measure μGibbs\mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}} is well-defined, and there exist deterministic almost sure limits

  2. (b)

5. Replica-symmetric overlaps and free energy

In this section, we prove Theorem 2.6 on the asymptotic overlaps and free energy of the Gibbs measure (2.8).

The argument is to establish a Markovian approximation of the generalized Langevin equation (2.2), using the fluctuation-dissipation relation between cg,rgc_{g},r_{g} in Lemma 4.2, an approximation of cg0​(τ)=cg​(τ)−lims→∞cg​(s)c_{g}^{0}(\tau)=c_{g}(\tau)-\lim_{s\to\infty}c_{g}(s) by the correlation function of observables of the lifted Markovian process 𝝃t={𝜽s}s∈[t−B,t]\boldsymbol{\xi}^{t}=\{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}\}_{s\in[t-B,t]} over path histories, a further approximation of this correlation function by a kernel c~g\tilde{c}_{g} defined via a finite-dimensional approximation of its infinitesimal generator, and a stable coupling between the dynamics driven by cg0c_{g}^{0} and c~g\tilde{c}_{g}.

The approximation of cg0c_{g}^{0} (and its derivative −rg{-}r_{g}) is carried out in the following lemma.

=O⁡(|β−β0|1+ρ+|β−β0|(N+1)​ρ)=o⁡(|β−β0|),\displaystyle=O(|\beta-\beta_{0}|^{1+\rho}+|\beta-\beta_{0}|^{(N+1)\rho})=o(|\beta-\beta_{0}|),

limn→∞1n​log⁡𝒵=f⁡(0,v∗​(0),q∗​(0))+∫01dd​β​f​(β,v∗​(β),q∗​(β))​𝑑β=f⁡(1,v∗​(1),q∗​(1)).\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log\mathcal{Z}=f(0,v_{*}(0),q_{*}(0))+\int_{0}^{1}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\beta}f(\beta,v_{*}(\beta),q_{*}(\beta))\mathrm{d}\beta=f(1,v_{*}(1),q_{*}(1)).

6. Universality over the disorder

We prove Corollary 2.10 on universality over the disorder 𝐗\mathbf{X}, using the results of [71].

Proof of Corollary 2.10.

Let 𝐗~∈ℝn×n\tilde{\mathbf{X}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} satisfy Assumption 2.9. Let 𝐗∈ℝn×n\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} be an orthogonally-invariant matrix satisfying Assumption 2.1 with the same bound Λmax\Lambda_{\max} and asymptotic eigenvalue distribution Λ\Lambda as 𝐗~\tilde{\mathbf{X}}. Let 𝐒∈ℝn×n\mathbf{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} be a random diagonal sign matrix as in Corollary 2.10(d), and let 𝚷∈ℝn×n\boldsymbol{\Pi}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} be a uniformly random permutation matrix, where (𝐒,𝚷)(\mathbf{S},\boldsymbol{\Pi}) are independent of each other and of 𝜽0,{𝐛t}t≥0\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0},\{\mathbf{b}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0}. Then [71, Proposition 2.7, Theorem 2.8] implies that the AMP algorithm (3.35) applied with 𝐗~\tilde{\mathbf{X}} has the same dynamical mean-field limit (3.37) (in the sense of almost-sure Wasserstein-2 convergence of the coordinatewise empirical distribution of its iterates) as applied with the matrix

𝐖=𝚷​𝐒​𝐗~​𝐒​𝚷⊤.\mathbf{W}=\boldsymbol{\Pi}\mathbf{S}\tilde{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{S}\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\top}.

As (3.37) and the bound ‖𝐗‖op≤Λmax\|\mathbf{X}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\Lambda_{\max} are the only properties of 𝐗\mathbf{X} used in all preceding proofs, this implies that Theorems 2.4, 2.6 and Corollaries 2.7, 2.8 hold equally with 𝐖\mathbf{W} in place of 𝐗\mathbf{X}.

The dynamics (2.1) driven by 𝐖\mathbf{W} have the form

d​𝜽t=[f⁡(𝜽t)+𝚷​𝐒​𝐗~​𝐒​𝚷⊤​𝜽t]​d​t+2​γ​d​𝐛t.\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}=[f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t})+\boldsymbol{\Pi}\mathbf{S}\tilde{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{S}\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}]\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{b}^{t}.

Define 𝐠t=𝐖​𝜽t−∫0trg​(t−s)​𝜽s​𝑑s\mathbf{g}^{t}=\mathbf{W}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}-\int_{0}^{t}r_{g}(t-s)\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}\mathrm{d}s as in Theorem 2.4, and let

The conclusion of Theorem 2.4 for {(𝜽t,𝐠t,𝐛t)}t≥0\{(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t},\mathbf{g}^{t},\mathbf{b}^{t})\}_{t\geq 0} implies the same convergence for {(𝜽~t,𝐠~t,𝐛~t)}t≥0\{(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t},\tilde{\mathbf{g}}^{t},\tilde{\mathbf{b}}^{t})\}_{t\geq 0}, since this has the same empirical distribution of sample paths. Multiplying the above dynamics by 𝚷⊤\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\top} and noting that 𝚷⊤​f​(𝜽t)=f⁡(𝜽~t)\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\top}f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t})=f(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t}) since f:ℝ→ℝf:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is applied entrywise, the dynamics of {(𝜽~t,𝐠~t,𝐛~t)}t≥0\{(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t},\tilde{\mathbf{g}}^{t},\tilde{\mathbf{b}}^{t})\}_{t\geq 0} are given by

(6.1) d​𝜽~t=[f⁡(𝜽~t)+𝐒​𝐗~​𝐒​𝜽~t]​𝑑t+2​γ​d​𝐛~t,𝐠~t=𝐒​𝐗~​𝐒​𝜽~t−∫0trg​(t−s)​𝜽~s​𝑑s,\mathrm{d}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t}=[f(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t})+\mathbf{S}\tilde{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{S}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t}]\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{\mathbf{b}}^{t},\qquad\tilde{\mathbf{g}}^{t}=\mathbf{S}\tilde{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{S}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t}-\int_{0}^{t}r_{g}(t-s)\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{s}\mathrm{d}s,

coinciding with the dynamics (2.1) driven by 𝐒​𝐗~​𝐒\mathbf{S}\tilde{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{S}. This shows Corollary 2.10(d) for the dynamics. Since the Gibbs measures μGibbs\mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}} and μIsing\mu_{\text{Ising}} defined by 𝐖\mathbf{W} are also identical to those defined by 𝐒​𝐗~​𝐒\mathbf{S}\tilde{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{S}, Corollary 2.10(d) holds also for the Gibbs measures.

If f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot) is odd and θ0\theta^{0} is sign-invariant in law, then the joint law of {(θt,gt,bt)}t≥0\{(\theta^{t},g^{t},b^{t})\}_{t\geq 0} in the dynamical mean-field limit of Definition 2.3 is also invariant under multiplication by a single sign s∈{±1}s\in\{\pm 1\}. Setting

𝜽~t=𝐒​𝚷⊤​𝜽t,𝐠~t=𝐒​𝚷⊤​𝐠t,𝐛~t=𝐒​𝚷⊤​𝐛t,\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t}=\mathbf{S}\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t},\qquad\tilde{\mathbf{g}}^{t}=\mathbf{S}\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\top}\mathbf{g}^{t},\qquad\tilde{\mathbf{b}}^{t}=\mathbf{S}\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\top}\mathbf{b}^{t},

the conclusion of Theorem 2.4 for {(𝜽t,𝐠t,𝐛t)}t≥0\{(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t},\mathbf{g}^{t},\mathbf{b}^{t})\}_{t\geq 0} implies that the empirical distribution of sample paths of {(𝜽~t,𝐠~t,𝐛~t)}t≥0\{(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t},\tilde{\mathbf{g}}^{t},\tilde{\mathbf{b}}^{t})\}_{t\geq 0} converges to the law of {(s​θt,s​gt,s​bt)}t≥0\{(s\theta^{t},sg^{t},sb^{t})\}_{t\geq 0} where s∈{±1}s\in\{\pm 1\} is an independent and uniformly random sign. This is the same law as that of {(θt,gt,bt)}t≥0\{(\theta^{t},g^{t},b^{t})\}_{t\geq 0}, so Theorem 2.4 holds also for {(𝜽~t,𝐠~t,𝐛~t)}t≥0\{(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t},\tilde{\mathbf{g}}^{t},\tilde{\mathbf{b}}^{t})\}_{t\geq 0}. Since 𝐒​𝚷⊤​f​(𝜽t)=f⁡(𝐒​𝚷⊤​𝜽t)=f⁡(𝜽~t)\mathbf{S}\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\top}f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t})=f(\mathbf{S}\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t})=f(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t}) when f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot) is odd, we have

d​𝜽~t=[f⁡(𝜽~t)+𝐗~​𝜽~t]​𝑑t+2​γ​d​𝐛~t,𝐠~t=𝐗~​𝜽~t−∫0trg​(t−s)​𝜽~s​𝑑s\mathrm{d}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t}=[f(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t})+\tilde{\mathbf{X}}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t}]\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{\mathbf{b}}^{t},\qquad\tilde{\mathbf{g}}^{t}=\tilde{\mathbf{X}}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t}-\int_{0}^{t}r_{g}(t-s)\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{s}\mathrm{d}s

coinciding with the dynamics (2.1) driven by 𝐗~\tilde{\mathbf{X}}. This shows Corollary 2.10(a). If U⁡(⋅)U(\cdot) is even and h=0h=0 in the Ising model, then the Gibbs measures μGibbs\mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}} and μIsing\mu_{\text{Ising}} defined by 𝐖\mathbf{W} are also identical to those defined by 𝐗~\tilde{\mathbf{X}}, implying Corollary 2.10(b–c). ∎

Appendix A Free cumulant bound

Proposition A.1.

Suppose Λ\Lambda is a random variable with |Λ|≤K|\Lambda|\leq K for a constant K>0K>0. Let {κp}p≥1\{\kappa_{p}\}_{p\geq 1} be the free cumulants of Λ\Lambda. Then

lim supp→∞|κp|1/p≤2​K.\limsup_{p\to\infty}|\kappa_{p}|^{1/p}\leq 2K.
Proof.

By rescaling Λ\Lambda, assume without loss of generality K=1K=1. For z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C} outside the support of Λ\Lambda, define the Cauchy transform 𝒢Λ​(z)=𝔼⁡[1/(z−Λ)]\mathcal{G}_{\Lambda}(z)=\mathbb{E}[1/(z-\Lambda)]. It is shown in [53, Theorem 17] that 𝒢Λ\mathcal{G}_{\Lambda} is univalent over {z:|z|>4}\{z:|z|>4\}, that {w:|w|∈(0,1/6)}⊂𝒢Λ​({z:|z|>4})\{w:|w|\in(0,1/6)\}\subset\mathcal{G}_{\Lambda}(\{z:|z|>4\}), and that ℛΛ​(w)\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(w) defined by (2.13) is absolutely convergent for |w|<1/6|w|<1/6 and given by

(A.1) ℛΛ​(w)=𝒢Λ−1​(w)−1w​ for ​|w|∈(0,1/6)\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(w)=\mathcal{G}_{\Lambda}^{-1}(w)-\frac{1}{w}\text{ for }|w|\in(0,1/6)

where 𝒢Λ−1​(w)\mathcal{G}_{\Lambda}^{-1}(w) denotes the unique inverse in {z:|z|>4}\{z:|z|>4\}.

We check that ℛΛ\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda} extends analytically to |w|<1/2|w|<1/2: Define, on the open disk 𝔻={z:|z|<1}\mathbb{D}=\{z:|z|<1\}, the analytic function

H⁡(z)=𝒢Λ​(1/z)=𝔼⁡[z/(1−z​Λ)].H(z)=\mathcal{G}_{\Lambda}(1/z)=\mathbb{E}[z/(1-z\Lambda)].

For any z∈𝔻z\in\mathbb{D} and |Λ|≤1|\Lambda|\leq 1, note that |1−z​Λ|2≤1+Λ2−2​ℜ⁡[z]​Λ≤(2+ε)​(1−ℜ⁡[z]​Λ)|1-z\Lambda|^{2}\leq 1+\Lambda^{2}-2\Re[z]\Lambda\leq(2+\varepsilon)(1-\Re[z]\Lambda). Then ℜ⁡[1/(1−z​Λ)]=(1−ℜ⁡[z]​Λ)/|1−z​Λ|2≥1/(2+ε)\Re[1/(1-z\Lambda)]=(1-\Re[z]\Lambda)/|1-z\Lambda|^{2}\geq 1/(2+\varepsilon). This implies 𝔼⁡[1/(1−z​Λ)]≠0\mathbb{E}[1/(1-z\Lambda)]\neq 0, so z=0z=0 is the unique simple root of H⁡(z)H(z) on 𝔻\mathbb{D}. Furthermore,

|H⁡(z)|≥|z|⋅ℜ⁡𝔼⁡[1/(1−z​Λ)]≥1−ε2+ε​ for ​|z|=1−ε.|H(z)|\geq|z|\cdot\Re\,\mathbb{E}[1/(1-z\Lambda)]\geq\frac{1-\varepsilon}{2+\varepsilon}\text{ for }|z|=1-\varepsilon.

Then by Rouché’s theorem, for each w∈ℂw\in\mathbb{C} with |w|<(1−ε)/(2+ε)|w|<(1-\varepsilon)/(2+\varepsilon), H⁡(z)=wH(z)=w also has a unique simple root zz in the disk {z:|z|<1−ε}\{z:|z|<1-\varepsilon\}. Since H′​(z)≠0H^{\prime}(z)\neq 0 at this root, the inverse function theorem implies that there exists an analytic inverse H−1H^{-1} on {w:|w|<(1−ε)/(2+ε)}\{w:|w|<(1-\varepsilon)/(2+\varepsilon)\}. Since H−1​(0)=0H^{-1}(0)=0, we have |H−1​(w)|<1/4|H^{-1}(w)|<1/4 on some neighborhood 𝒪\mathcal{O} of w=0w=0, and 𝒢Λ​(1/H−1​(w))=H⁡(H−1​(w))=w\mathcal{G}_{\Lambda}(1/H^{-1}(w))=H(H^{-1}(w))=w. Then the above univalence implies 1/H−1​(w)=𝒢Λ−1​(w)1/H^{-1}(w)=\mathcal{G}_{\Lambda}^{-1}(w) for all w∈𝒪w\in\mathcal{O}. Then the right side of (A.1) has an analytic extension to {w:|w|∈(0,(1−ε)/(2+ε))}\{w:|w|\in(0,(1-\varepsilon)/(2+\varepsilon))\}. Since ε>0\varepsilon>0 is arbitrary, this implies ℛΛ​(w)\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(w) extends analytically to |w|<1/2|w|<1/2, as claimed. Then ℛΛ​(w)\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(w) is given by the convergent series (2.13) for all |w|<1/2|w|<1/2, so the root test implies that lim supp→∞|κp|1/p≤2\limsup_{p\to\infty}|\kappa_{p}|^{1/p}\leq 2. ∎

Statement on AI use

Several supporting proof ideas were obtained in dialogue with ChatGPT (GPT-5.5) over the course of this research: the Gaussian coupling construction of Corollary 5.2, the Gaussian mixture interpolation of Corollary 2.8, the extension from Hölder-continuity to continuous-differentiability concluding the proof of Theorem 2.6(b), and the free cumulant bound of Proposition A.1. The authors assume responsibility for the correctness of all stated results.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
